parts.title: Renting a stall at a craft market
parts.context: A woman who makes candles phones the organiser of a craft market.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning the organiser of a craft market about renting a stall. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: dawson
script.text: Riverside Craft Market, John Dawson speaking.

script.speaker: kate
script.text: Hello. I make candles, and I'm interested in having a stall at the market. Could you tell me what kinds of stall you have?

script.speaker: dawson
script.text: Of course. There are three kinds. The standard stall is two metres wide.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: A standard stall is two metres wide, so '2 metres wide' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: dawson
script.text: The standard stall costs twenty-five pounds a day, and that includes the use of one table. Most people find that's enough.

script.speaker: kate
script.text: And the bigger ones?

script.speaker: dawson
script.text: The large stall is four metres wide, and it's forty pounds. As well as a table, you get electricity, which is useful if you want to put up lights.

script.speaker: kate
script.text: Hmm, lights might show off the candles nicely. And the third kind?

script.speaker: dawson
script.text: That's the covered stall. It's three metres wide, inside the old market hall, so you're out of the rain. That one's thirty-five pounds.

script.speaker: kate
script.text: I see. I think I'll go for the covered one. Candles don't like getting wet.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: kate
script.text: When is the market held?

script.speaker: dawson
script.text: On the first Sunday of every month. It used to be on Saturdays, but we moved it so that it doesn't clash with the farmers' market.

script.speaker: kate
script.text: And what time do I need to be there?

script.speaker: dawson
script.text: The market opens to the public at nine, but stallholders must arrive by seven, so that everything is ready in time.

script.speaker: kate
script.text: Can I park next to my stall?

script.speaker: dawson
script.text: You can unload there, but after that, all cars have to be moved to the car park behind the library. It's free on Sundays.

script.speaker: kate
script.text: That's fine. Is there anything else I need?

script.speaker: dawson
script.text: Yes, every stallholder needs public liability insurance. We can't let you trade without it, I'm afraid.

script.speaker: kate
script.text: I already have that. How do I apply?

script.speaker: dawson
script.text: Just fill in the form on our website. We like to keep a good mix of crafts, so we also ask everyone to email some photographs of what they make.

script.speaker: kate
script.text: No problem. I'll do that this evening. Thank you.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Changes to household waste collection
parts.context: A local radio presenter explains a town's new system for collecting household waste.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a local radio presenter talking about changes to household waste collection. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: Good morning. Many of you have been asking about the new waste collection scheme here in Harbridge, so I've been finding out the details. The scheme was supposed to start on the first of March, but delivery of the new bins was delayed, so it'll now begin on the first of April.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: Why is it happening? Some people think it's just about saving money, and the council admits it will save a little. But the main reason is that the government has set a national target for recycling, and at the moment Harbridge is a long way below it.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: So how will collections work? Food waste will be collected every week, and recycling every two weeks, as now. But general waste, that's the black bin, will only be collected every three weeks.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: And what about your old bins? Please don't take them to the recycling centre yourself. Just put a sticker on them and leave them out on your usual collection day, and they'll be taken away.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: There's good news about what you can recycle. From April, you can put drink cartons and plastic food trays in the blue bin. Glass bottles could always go in, of course. Plastic bags still can't, I'm afraid, and batteries must never go in any of your bins, because they can start fires in the lorries.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: Every home will also get a small food caddy for the kitchen. The caddies are free, and you can buy special bags to line them, though wrapping food in newspaper works just as well. You can put in all kinds of food, cooked or raw, including meat, bones and even pet food.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: If you'd like more information, there is a phone line, but it's going to be very busy for the first few weeks. The easiest way is to use the council website, where you can type in your postcode and see your collection days.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: And finally, what happens if you put the wrong things in your bin? Nobody will be fined, at least not at first. But if the crew find the wrong items, your bin won't be emptied, and they'll attach a tag explaining why.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A survey of commuters
parts.context: Two students discuss the results of their survey on how people travel to work.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two students, Leo and Priya, discussing a survey they did on how people travel to work. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: Leo, I think the survey went really well. I'm glad we did it face to face in the town centre and not online.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: Me too. Online, we'd mostly have reached students like us. In the town centre we got a much wider range of ages, including a lot of older people.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: And people were so friendly. I thought lots of them would refuse to stop, but hardly anyone did.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: The rain on the first day wasn't a problem either, because we stood under the shopping centre roof. The only real problem was on the second morning, when we ran out of question sheets and had to go back and print more.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: Yes, that was annoying. Now, the results. We asked people why they chose their way of travelling. I really expected cost to be the top reason.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: So did I, and speed came second. But the number one answer was reliability. People just want to know they'll arrive on time.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: And then the cyclists. Most of them were under thirty, which is what we expected. What we didn't expect was that they had the longest journeys of all, more than eight kilometres on average.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: And they weren't any happier than bus users, which also surprised me.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: So what should we recommend in the report? More bike lanes?

script.speaker: leo
script.text: They're already planned, and bus fares are set by the bus company, not the council. I think the most useful thing the council could actually do is put screens at bus stops showing when the next bus is coming.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: Good. Let's make that our main recommendation.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: Let's go through the findings for each kind of transport. The bus was the most popular with people over sixty, mainly because they can travel free.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: And the train was delayed most often, about one journey in four, according to the people we asked.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: The drivers spent the most money each month, mostly on parking in the town centre.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: The people who walked to work said they mainly did it for their health. Lots of them had been told to by their doctor.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: And the number of people cycling has doubled since the last survey five years ago, so it's growing faster than anything else.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: Right. Let's put all that in a table.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the invention of the tin can
parts.context: A lecture on the history of preserving food in cans.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the history of the tin can. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good afternoon. Today's lecture is about an invention that changed how the whole world eats, but that most of us never think about: the tin can.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The story starts in France at the end of the eighteenth century. France was at war, and keeping soldiers fed far from home was a huge problem, so the government offered a prize for a new way to preserve food for the army.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The winner was a cook and sweet-maker called Nicolas Appert. After years of experiments, he found that if he sealed food in glass bottles and then heated them in boiling water, the food stayed fresh for months. Nobody, including Appert, understood why it worked.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The method had one big weakness. Glass is heavy, and on long journeys the containers often broke.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The solution came from England. In eighteen ten, a merchant called Peter Durand was given a patent for a container made of iron coated with tin. Within a few years, a factory in London was supplying canned meat and vegetables to the navy and to explorers.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Strangely, nobody had invented a way to open them. Early cans were so thick that the instructions told people to cut round the top with a hammer and chisel. Soldiers sometimes used their bayonets, or even shot them open. The can opener was only invented almost fifty years later, once cans had become thinner.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: It was the French scientist Louis Pasteur who finally explained why canning worked. In the eighteen sixties he showed that food goes bad because of tiny living organisms, which we now call bacteria. Heating kills them, and the sealed can stops new ones getting in.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: There were dangers too. The seams of early cans were sealed with lead, which could slowly poison the people eating from them, and some historians believe this harmed polar explorers who lived on canned food for years.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Today's cans are made of steel or aluminium, and the inside is usually lined with a very thin layer of plastic, so that the metal doesn't affect the taste of the food. And they are among the most recycled packaging in the world.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
